articles.headline: The Bad Lands Cow Boy.
articles.text:
Volume 2, Number 10. MEDORA, DAKOTA, APRIL 9, 1885. PRICE $2.00 PER YEAR.

BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD.

THE COW BOY is not published for fun, but for $2 per year.
Advertising Rates made known on application.
Standing Advertisements payable quarterly.
Transient Advertisements and all Job work, money in sight.
Address all communications to THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, MEDORA, DAKOTA.

Entered at the post-office at Medora, Dak., as second class mail matter.
articles.summary: Masthead and publisher's box for Vol. 2, No. 10, Medora, April 9, 1885. (A pasted subscriber's mailing label on the scan reads "Marquise de Mores, 272 Madison Ave, New York City N Y".)

articles.text: As before announced, next Wednesday, April 15 has been set apart by the Governor, as Arbor day. Those wishing to help along the good work by planting trees are requested to come to the Cow Boy office before Sunday to talk the matter up and make preparations for a meeting.
articles.summary: Arbor Day set for Wednesday, April 15; tree planters asked to meet at the Cow Boy office before Sunday.

articles.text: We do not know for what good deeds we are being rewarded by this perfect weather. From exchanges all over the United States we judge that we are having about the only good weather prevalent anywhere. For the last four weeks it has been simply perfect. There is no rose without its thorn, though, and we are now wishing for rain.
articles.summary: Four weeks of perfect weather; the town now wishes for rain.

articles.text: The bull round-up south of the track begins next Monday. The one north of the track began last Tuesday and has already worked Knutson creek and the adjacent country. South of the track, Ferris & Merrifield's ranch will be a head-quarters until that vicinity has been worked, when the camps will be moved farther up the river, gradually working the whole country.
articles.summary: Bull round-up north of the track began Tuesday; the one south of the track starts Monday, headquartered at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch.

articles.text: It may be blowing our own horn, but we wish to assert that Medora is and has been for some time the best town on the road for its size. It is almost impossible to find an idle man and those who are idle from choice are soon asked to seek a more congenial clime. We havn't had a boom and don't one. No business has been overdone, there have been no failures and everyone is presperous.
articles.summary: Packard boasts Medora is the best town on the road for its size, with no idle men and no business failures.

articles.text: Although it is almost impossible to get accurate information from the seat of war in the Saskatchewan country, all reports seem to indicate that Riel has a large body of troops who are liable to give the Dominion soldiers much trouble on account of their superior arms marksmanship and bushwhacking mode of fighting. The man Riel has left a reputation wherever he has gone of being a two-faced rascal but he is now at the head of a good cause and it is to be hoped that it will be successful.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on the Riel rising in the Saskatchewan country.

articles.text: The latest news from the bedside of Gen. Grant is that he may linger for several months or he may die in a few days. Universal sympathy is felt for the dying hero and papers which formerly villified him in every possible way on account of partizan feeling are now [illegible] of his good qualities. He is now living simply on account of his immense will power and the determination not to give up.
articles.summary: Editorial note on the illness of Gen. U. S. Grant.

articles.headline: Stock Statistics.
articles.text:
We are in receipt of the report of the department of Agriculture in reference to numbers and values of farm animals which contains many valuable statistics. From it, we learn that the January returns on horses and mules show an increase of four per cent. Especially in the territories, where much attention has been given to horse breeding, is this increase manifest.

For the United States the increase for the year has been 391,889 on horses, the present number being 11,564,572.

In cattle there has been an increase of 820,472 the present number being 29,866,573. The average value of horses for 1885 is $93.70 being a decrease of ninety-four cents. The average price of cattle is $23.02, being a decrease of fifty cents. The total value of the horses in the United States is $852,282,927 and the total value of cattle is $694,382,913. The total value of all domestic animals is $2,456,425,933.

The pamphlet also contains many valuable tables, showing numbers and values of animals in different states and territories. By these, it appears that in cattle, Texas heads the list with 66,784,736, Montana comes thirteenth, with 17,324,550 and Dakota fifteenth with 11,001,649.

The price of beef in Chicago was highest in 1882, when extra beeves sold at $9.15 to $9.40 and choice were $8.65 to $8.90. On Jan. 1, 1884, extra beeves sold at $7.00 to $7.25, choice for $6.30 to $6.40 and medium for $4.50 to $5.00. On Jan. 1, 1885, the prices were $6.65 to $6.85 for extra, $6.25 to $6.60 for choice and $5.00 to $5.50 for medium.

It appears that sheep have increased in Dakota less than one per cent., "accounted for by the low price of wool and that so many tag-end and scrub flocks were shipped in from the east two years ago and did so poorly for their masters. It has also been proved that the ordinary breed of sheep need more care than flock-masters thought necessary to give them."

Animals in the northern part of the territory are valued higher than those in the southern part, horses and mules being of a better class.

Texas and Dakota have more cattle than all of Europe combined.

In the last pages of the pan[ph]let are freight rates, rail and water, to and from all the prominent shipping points, containing valuable information to all those intending to ship cattle in any direction.
articles.summary: Summary of a Department of Agriculture report on livestock numbers, values and beef prices.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice of a bay horse belonging to John Pohl strayed or stolen from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884; $25 reward.

articles.headline: Meeting of the Montana Stock-grower's Association.
articles.text:
FRIDAY MORNING SESSION.

The annual spring meeting of the Eastern Montana Live Stock association was called to order by chairman Bryan at 11:10 last Friday morning. The chairman made a few remarks to the effect that two years ago the association consisted of seven members and met in a little back room but now the largest hall in the city was scarcely able to seat the association and its friends who had come to the meeting.

Fifty-seven new names were read for membership and with one exception were unanimously elected by the secretary's ballot.

A conference committee on consolidation was appointed to meet one from the other association already appointed. Adjourned.

FRIDAY AFTERNOON SESSION.

At three o'clock, chairmam Bryan called the convention to order and appointed a districting committee which together with the north side members, should form round-up districts. Among the rest, John Goodall was appointed for the Little Missouri, Henry Boice for Beaver and A. Cole for Glendive.

Messrs. Green and Burleigh were appointed a committee to draft a memorial to the secretary of war to allow the erection of stock-yards on the Ft. Keogh reservation.

After a few remarks on the Indian question by which nothing definite was reached the meeting adjourned.

FRIDAY EVENING'S SESSION.

About eight o'clock the meeting was called to order by chairman Bryan who stated that the conference committees on consolidation were ready to report.

In brief the report was entirely in favor of consolidation. That the name be changed to the Montana Stockgrower's association, that the executive committe[e] [consist?] of twenty-five members [illegible] Dakota shall have two, that the annual dues shall be $10, that the association meet semi-annually and that the spring meeting be in Miles City and the fall meeting in Helena. The report was unanimously adopted.

The by-laws of the new association were then read and in brief are as follows: That the name of this association be the Montana Stockgrower's Association, that its object is in every way to advance stock interests in Mantana and adjoining territories, that the officers shall be a President, 1st. Vice-President 2nd. Vice-President, Secretary and Treasure combined and an Executive committee, all these officers to be elected on the first day of the semi-annual meeting in April. No person can become a member, except he be a stockgrower, defined as follows: A person owning or controlling cattle, horses, mules or asses and engaged in the business of herding, growing and raising the same for profit. By a very forcible speech of Gov. Potts and the hearty concurrence of the association, the bad custom of electing honorary members was done away with. Membership shall also be personal and not by firms. The entrance fee shall be fifteen dollars, the annual dues ten dollars, and and all members are subject to an assessment, not oftener than annual, of one cent a head on not over seventy per cent. of all his stock.

The following officers were then unanimously elected:

President—Col. T. J. Bryan.
1st Vice President—Gov. B. F. Potts.
2nd Vice President—Capt. Wm. Harmon.
Secretary and Treasurer—R. B. Harrison.

EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE.

Beaverhead County—Dr. Azel Ames, Jr.
Choteau County—Jesse Taylor, R. P. Walker, John Lepley.
Custer County—Joe Scott, Frank Robertson, E. S. Newman, J. J. Thompson.
Dawson County—J. S. Day, David Hunter.
Deer Lodge County—Conrad Kohrs.
Gallatin County—Charles Aucency.
Jefferson County—S. S. Huntley.
Lewis and Clarke County—J. T. Murphy, R. S. Hamilton.
Madison County—Alex. Metzel.
Meagher County—Granville Stuart, S. S. Hobson, J. H. Freezer.
Missoula County—C. P. Higgins.
Silver Bow County—Nicholas Bielenberg.
Yellowstone County—Sam. Garvin, A. A. Ellis.
Dakota Territory—Marquis De Mores Jno. N. Simpson.

On motion a vote of thanks tendered to Hon. Granville Stewart and R. B. Harrison for efficient work done at Helena during the meeting of the legislature. Secretary R. B. Harrison then read a report on bulls which we are sorry not to be able to publish. It was a masterly and logical production proving conclusively that there is no economy in cheap bulls or a small number and that all bulls should be taken from the range on or about Nov. 1st and not again put on the range before June or July.

The round-up committee then reported, the Little Missouri, being district six. It begins May 25 at the mouth of Box Elder, thence working down the Little Missouri and its tributaries to a point about twenty miles below the mouth of Big Beaver, thence up Big Beaver and its tributaries to the Northern Pacific. Wal. T. Osterhaut was appointed foreman.

The report of the secretary and treasurer of the E. M. L. S. association was read and approved. It showed a balance on hand of $396.78. After all debts were paid and assessments collected there would be $22.46 on hand.

A standing committee on membership, consisting of R. S. Hamilton, J. J. Thompson, J. T. Murphy and R. B. Harrison, was appointed to whom applications could be sent and who were empowered to enrol any person as a member without a vote of the association.

Adjourned.
articles.summary: Report of the Miles City meeting at which the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association consolidated into the Montana Stockgrower's Association; de Mores named to the executive committee for Dakota; Little Missouri round-up (district six) set for May 25 under foreman Wal. T. Osterhaut.

articles.text: Our cowmen are well pleased at the incorporation of the western part of Dakota in the Montana territorial association. For some time we will be too weak to stand alone and by joining the Montana association we become a prominent part of what two years hence will be the strongest stock organization in the world.
articles.summary: Local cowmen welcome western Dakota's inclusion in the Montana association.

articles.text: The following was sent us by W. A. VanBrunt, president of the Badger cattle Co.: "A Paulding farmer having cattle trespassing upon his grain fields, posted up the following: 'Notis—If any man's or woman's cows or oxen gits in these here otes his or her tale will be off as the cass may be. I am a Christian and pay mi taxes, darn a man who lets his critter run luse, say i.'"
articles.summary: Humorous trespass notice sent in by W. A. VanBrunt of the Badger Cattle Co.

articles.text: The Texas cattlemen are in really desperate straits on account of the quarantine laws. It is impossible for all of them to find a market for their cattle and sales at low figures are made wherever opportunity offers. Many of the Texas cowmen are working on borrowed money and pay-day will find them entirely unprepared to square up. It is thought that more cattlemen will be closed out there this year than ever before.
articles.summary: Texas cattlemen in desperate straits because of quarantine laws.

articles.text: While in Miles City we spoke with a large number in reference to Texas fever and all agreed, even though some had [large interests in Texas, that the fever?] was by no means a scare. Several illustrations were cited where a Texas trail had been crossed by states cattle and every animal in the latter herd had died. Our best authority seemed to think that the name Texas fever was a mis-nomer for the same deadly disease arises when cattle are driven continually from one point to another. This rule he claimed to be nearly or quite without exception, the disease with the same symptoms having arisen on every well used trail the world over.
articles.summary: Packard reports Miles City cattlemen's views that Texas fever is a real danger.

articles.text: More and more are the cowmen beginning to realize that talk will do no good and that if they expect to have the proper per cent. of calves, each member of the different associations must be forced to put in the requisite number of bulls. This is a question that admits of no farther delay and one that must be immediately and strictly enforced. Where is the business man in the world but would add five per cent. to his capital stock if by so doing it were conclusively proved that he would gain fifteen per cent? The case is exactly as plain in the matter of a full supply of bulls and still a large number of cowmen havn't their proper proportion. We may as well come out flat-footed and state what is a notorious fact, that these men expect to gain the fifteen per cent. profit without the five per cent addition to the capital stock. Our association was very decided in this matter and it was fully decided to make every man on the river put in his required number. Some may still try to sponge off their neighbors and a close watch should be kept to see that the letter of the law is strictly enforced.
articles.summary: Editorial urging that every Little Missouri cowman put in his required number of bulls, as the local association has decided.

articles.text: Some one has been writing to the Kansas City Live Stock Indicator objecting to polled cattle on the ground that the muley cow and calf on the plains will fall easy prey to the wolves on account of the absence of the pointed weapons worn by the Texas cow. Another correspondent and friend of the blacks says: "We respectfully refer J. P. S. W. to Prof. E. M. Shelton, whose testimony should quiet his apprehension in this matter. Says the observant and experienced professor, in speaking of muleys—'moreover they strike viciously with their mallet-shaped heads.' Those of us who have handled hornless beasts know that the sight of a dog will arouse warlike demonstrations on the part of the muley quicker than anything else, and it is an acknowleged fact that, although peaceable by nature, when it does come to the tug of war a muley will thump the everlasting daylights out of anything that wears hoofs and horns. Taking these two facts into consideration, it is reasonable to suppose that the howling wolf and the screeching coyote of the wild west will quickly learn to respect the butting bump on the mallet-shaped muley head."—[Stockgrower's Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Stockgrower's Journal defending polled (muley) cattle against wolves.

articles.text: BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD. THURSDAY, APRIL 9, 1885.
articles.summary: Page-4 editorial masthead dated Thursday, April 9, 1885.

articles.text: Mrs. Lason has been very sick but the chances now are that she will recover.
articles.summary: Mrs. Lason has been very sick but is expected to recover.

articles.text: The orange racee at th rink to-night will be contested for by ladies exclusively.
articles.summary: Ladies-only orange race at the rink tonight.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin came up night before last and celebrated mass this morning.
articles.summary: Father Martin arrived and celebrated mass.

articles.text: Jack McGregor came up from his ranch, the first of the week and left for home this morning.
articles.summary: Jack McGregor visited town from his ranch.

articles.text: Mrs. R.: "Oh, what a beautiful baby! it's the prettiest thing I ever saw and the exact image of its father." Gear faints.
articles.summary: A humorous squib about a baby.

articles.text: Father Martin has made arrangements with Jim Butler, by which new pews will soon adorn the Catholic church.
articles.summary: New pews arranged for the Catholic church.

articles.text: Again must the Gun club express its thanks to Lieut. Partello for his kindness in furnishing a bountiful supply of targets, pasters, etc.
articles.summary: Gun club thanks Lieut. Partello for targets.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores, John Goodall, Howard Eaton, J. L. Truscott, Wal. Osterhaut, Joe McCoul and A. T. Packard attended the Miles City meeting from Medora.
articles.summary: List of Medora men who attended the Miles City stockmen's meeting.

articles.text: Howard Eaton and Joe McCoul bought a number of cow-horses in Miles City. The most of them were bought for J. A. VanEeghan and will be kept here for sale.
articles.summary: Eaton and McCoul bought cow-horses in Miles City for J. A. VanEeghan.

articles.text: And now there is rejoicing in the house of Paddock. Tuesday afternoon there was born to Mrs. Paddock, a fourteen pound girl baby. The mother and child are both doing well.
articles.summary: A girl was born to Mrs. Paddock on Tuesday.

articles.text: Mr. Anderson, of the Drover's Journal, stopped off here Sunday on his way to Chicago, from the Miles City convention. Among stock dealers, he is probably the widest known man in the country.
articles.summary: Mr. Anderson of the Drover's Journal stopped at Medora Sunday.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens is putting up a new building for his drug store as his present quarters are too small. He will probably branch out into the crockery business. In a few days he will start for the Hills to attend to business matters there.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens is building a new drug store and will visit the Black Hills.

articles.text: It will be noticed that the new time table of the Northern Pacific is now in force. No. 1, going west, arrives at 6:47 p. m. and No. 2, going east, at 8:43 a. m. The emigrant train is again running, being freight No. 17, and arrives at 11:40.
articles.summary: New Northern Pacific time table in force; emigrant train running again.

articles.text: We have not the score of last Saturday's shoot and will now publish only the total scores when all the contestants have shot their full series. Nothing preventing, this will be done Saturday and the successful contestant will then be known.
articles.summary: Gun club shoot scores to be published when the series is complete.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher offers two prizes for the best scores made before May 1st. in his shooting gallery at the rink. A box of cigars will be given to the member of the Little Missouri Gun club making the best score in a hundred shots and a like prize to any person not a member. All shots to count. Ten shots for a quarter. All shooting to be off-hand.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher offers shooting prizes at the rink before May 1.

articles.text: Again has the decapitator been at work and the heads of Gen'l. M'n'g'r. Simpson and Superintendent Smith fall into the basket. We are sorry to see Mr. Smith go as he was a good stage man and agreeable gentleman. It would have been a sin, however, to keep Simpson, as the Dakota atmosphere fairly ruined the bloom of his ashes-of-roses or dregs-of-wine complexion.
articles.summary: General Manager Simpson and Superintendent Smith of the stage line have been removed.

articles.text: The brick work on the hotel will be almost completed this week and with the exception of the roof, will be as neat a looking building as could be wished. There will be two brick additions, one for the bar-room and the other for the kitchen. We understand that the porches have been taken from the plan. If so, it will take far more from the looks than the additional expense would have added. Peter Book is displaying his pressed brick to advantage and no better brick or brick-work can be found on the road.
articles.summary: Brick work on the new hotel nearly complete; Peter Book's pressed brick praised.

articles.text: Several persons from here learned from what was considered a reliable source in Miles City that John Warn had been sentenced at Bozeman to a year in the penitentiary. The reasons given, corresponded with those already known and as they were trivial and manifestly the work of enemies, a petition for his pardon to the governor of Montana was circulated here and numerously signed. It now turns out that John was only sentenced to thirty days through the efforts of his enemies and that he intends to "fight 'em, blood raw" at the end of his imprisonment.
articles.summary: John Warn, reported sentenced at Bozeman, received thirty days; Medora had circulated a pardon petition.

articles.text: Round-up begins May 25.
articles.summary: Round-up begins May 25.

articles.text: Geo. Porter and wife are still absent in Chicago.
articles.summary: Geo. Porter and wife remain in Chicago.

articles.text: B. F. Lamb returned from Bismarck last evening.
articles.summary: B. F. Lamb returned from Bismarck.

articles.text: A tasty gilt cross now adorns the steeple of the Catholic church.
articles.summary: A gilt cross placed on the Catholic church steeple.

articles.text: Mike Knott should be appointed to the position of "foreman of the stiff-firing gang."
articles.summary: Joke nominating Mike Knott foreman of the tramp-expelling gang.

articles.text: Mrs. J. D. Garver is quite ill in Bismarck and Mr. Garver went down this morning to attend her.
articles.summary: Mrs. J. D. Garver ill in Bismarck; her husband went to her.

articles.text: Dr. Robarts is kept busy, vibrating between Dickinson and Medora. He has number of patients in both places.
articles.summary: Dr. Robarts busy with patients in Dickinson and Medora.

articles.text: The grass is coming up in good shape and all that is needed now is two or thee days rain to give it a first-class start.
articles.summary: Grass coming up well; rain needed.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores and Wm. Van-[Driesche?] started east Tuesday morning William will return in a few days and the Marquis about the 23rd.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores and his man William left for the East Tuesday.

articles.text: W. B. Pryor is now started in good shape and prepared to do any work in the boot and shoe line. His advertisement will appear in the next Cow Boy.
articles.summary: W. B. Pryor opens a boot and shoe shop.

articles.text: Owing to the thoughtfulness of S. A. [illegible]arney, of the Stockgrower's, our editorial frame reclined on a downy bed while in Miles, where we might otherwise have had to rustle for a chair even so great was the crowd.
articles.summary: Packard thanks a Stockgrower's Journal man for lodging in crowded Miles City.

articles.text: The masquerade to take place at the rink the evening of April 15, bids fair to be even above the usual order of parties in pleasure. The doors will be open at 7:30, the grand march will begin at 9:30. No person not masked will be allowed on the floor until ten o'clock, when all will unmask. Dancing will then begin and continue until twelve. Tickets one dollar, children fifty cents. No improper characters admitted.
articles.summary: Masquerade ball at the rink set for April 15.

articles.text: For the first time in the history of the stage line, a coach tipped over. It occurred this side of Davis creek and ginned up the passengers pretty briskly. One, the Ft. Meade post trader, seemed to be hurt in the back, while Charlie Jolly, had a rib fractured and some of the muscles torn loose on his side. This was aggravated by the jolting of the coach and the hurt looked quite serious by the time he arrived here Charlie is now at Geo. Roderick's and resting easily.
articles.summary: A stage coach tipped over near Davis creek, injuring Charlie Jolly and the Ft. Meade post trader.

articles.text: Up and down the line the warning cry will soon be passed from mouth to mouth by all the bums, "Steer clear of Medora." This is a subject we have not hitherto mentioned, as we could not see that any good would be derived therefrom and the occasional process of "firing a stiff," was not altogether unenjoyable. Lately, however, what at times might be considered as a mild species of enjoyment under other circumstances, has now come to be a positive bore. The last stiff was fired Monday, being escorted out of town by two citizens. He was afterward pursued and brought back on a hand-car and acknowledged to stealing a lot of stage meal tickets. After several persons had used moral or other suasion on him, he was again escorted out of town. The treatment this man received was not altogether lamb-like, but by comparison with what others will receive, it certainly was. We want it distinctly understood that Medora is the unhealthiest place on the road for tramps and bums. There is scarcely an idle man in our busy little burg, loafing being an unknown art. We do not by any means intimate that honest working men are not wanted here. They are as welcome as spring showers and we doubt if a capable workman has ever yet sought here in vain for a job. But we do not want tramps and they will be fired out of town with an ever-increasing momentum liable to jar some of their finer sensibilities.
articles.summary: Editorial warning tramps to steer clear of Medora, after a tramp who stole stage meal tickets was run out of town Monday.
